scores.accuracy_concern: The 'more than two thirds' figure is correct arithmetic for hours (115.5 of 168 outside 08:00 to 18:30 weekdays) but hours are not demand, and England's enhanced access adds some evening and Saturday GP cover; the Scottish core-hours definition and any claim about when care home admissions start need their own source.
scores.sharpen: Build the checklist around the three things an out-of-hours reader needs in the first minute (what to do if unwell, what the person would not want, whom to phone) and drop the admissions-timing claim unless a source gives a figure.

scores.values_concern: Aim the criticism at commissioning and scheduling, not at care workers who work to the rota they are given.
scores.accuracy_concern: The EHRC 2011 and CQC 2013 reports are old and must be checked for specific findings on early bedtime visits; the ASCOF 'control over daily life' measure covers all social care users, not home care alone.
scores.sharpen: Anchor the post in one verified source that documents early bedtime visits and end on the exact question to raise at a care review about the time of the evening visit.

scores.accuracy_concern: The evidence leads (2010 to 2013) are marked unsure; the link between uninformed care workers and unwanted 999 calls needs a source or must be phrased as a risk, and ReSPECT is not used everywhere.
scores.sharpen: Replace the old, unsure leads with a recent review or UK study of home care workers in end-of-life care, and make the four-item 'share this with the agency' list the visual centrepiece.

scores.values_concern: Comparing with Sweden can read as a policy position; keep the post about the measure, not about the Swedish system.
scores.accuracy_concern: The Socialstyrelsen indicator and the national figure (thought to be around 15 to 16 staff in 14 days) must be verified from a citable document, which may be hard because official web pages could not be opened; 'the UK publishes nothing like it' is an absence claim that needs to be phrased as 'we found no national measure'.
scores.sharpen: Verify the current Swedish indicator and figure from a report or peer-reviewed paper before drafting, and keep the calendar grids clearly labelled as illustrative.

scores.values_concern: Must not imply that care workers take over tasks out of indifference; keep the time-pressure point prominent.
scores.accuracy_concern: The dependence-support script comes from observational studies from the 1980s and 1990s, and 'doing for' as a cause of lost ability is not established by trials; function-focused care trials show modest and mixed effects.
scores.sharpen: Drop the causal implication, lead with the care plan question, and cite one trial or review of function-focused care with its modest results stated.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Enhanced Health in Care Homes weekly 'home round' can be a remote check-in, and alignment does not mean every home meets the framework; the framework is England-only and Scotland's differs; the NHS England documents may not be openable.
scores.sharpen: Keep this as a family question card, separate from C16-29, and add what a good answer sounds like (a named practice, a regular clinical check, a stated route to therapists and a dentist).

scores.accuracy_concern: Responder rules vary by council and provider and there may be no national source, so the key premise rests on service pages; Fleming and Brayne studied people aged 90 and over in Cambridge, so do not generalise their figures to all older people.
scores.sharpen: Find one checkable national source (Age UK or the Telecare Services Association) that describes responder requirements, and add what someone with nobody nearby can ask for (a mobile response service, and whether it costs extra).

scores.values_concern: Can read as criticism of practice staff; present it as a test the practice runs on itself and acknowledge demand on reception teams.
scores.accuracy_concern: The share of people aged 75 and over who do not use the internet must come from a current Ofcom or ONS release; GP contract wording on access routes changed in 2025 and must be quoted exactly; overlaps with C17 digital exclusion.
scores.sharpen: Replace the composite 85-year-old with a named, repeatable test (ring at 08:00 with a hearing aid out, no online form) and verify the current non-user figure.

scores.values_concern: Must not present a care home move as a failure or home as always better; include what happens when the person lacks capacity for this decision.
scores.accuracy_concern: The decision belongs to the person only when they have capacity for it, otherwise a best-interests process applies; funding rules can constrain options; outcome comparisons between settings are confounded.
scores.sharpen: Give each list three verifiable items and add the capacity point in one line so readers know who decides when the person cannot.

scores.accuracy_concern: Boyd et al. 2008 found that many people did not recover to their pre-admission function within a year, so the recovery claim must be given with the non-recovery figure; the English discharge guidance was revised in 2022 and 2024 and must be quoted exactly; the interim-placement drift claim is unverified.
scores.sharpen: State Boyd 2008's recovery and non-recovery proportions side by side so the post neither promises recovery nor dismisses it, and quote the discharge guidance wording.

scores.accuracy_concern: The repeat-list mechanism is plausible and should be labelled as an illustrative sequence, not a measured frequency; the Discharge Medicines Service readmission findings come from service evaluations, not trials.
scores.sharpen: Add one named fix in a single line (who updates the repeat list, and by when, after the discharge letter arrives) and cite a study showing discharge medicine changes not carried into primary care records.

scores.values_concern: Survival statistics for care home residents can read as fatalistic; emphasise the wide spread and that many people live for years after moving in.
scores.accuracy_concern: Forder and Fernandez 2011 used older cohorts and stays may have shortened since; the higher mortality of care home residents reflects who moves in and must not be presented as an effect of the home.
scores.sharpen: Use a verified distribution from a recent UK linked-data study if one exists, and end on the question to ask the clinician about this person.

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying that staff who give settling-in advice are uncaring; frame it as a question families can ask.
scores.accuracy_concern: 'No good-quality evidence' needs a search of relocation-adjustment reviews to support it as an evidence gap; the premise that homes advise staying away needs a source; Regulation 9A allows restriction in some circumstances; the status and wording of Anne's Law in Scotland (Standards amended 2022, later legislation) must be checked.
scores.sharpen: Confirm first that reviews show no evidence for staying away and that the advice is actually given; otherwise reframe as 'agree visiting around what the person wants, before the move'.

scores.accuracy_concern: I STUMBLE items must be copied verbatim from the ambulance service source; evaluations of lifting equipment and post-fall tools are mostly local before-and-after data; long-lie harms are associations; residents with dementia may not report pain, which makes 'no injury' harder to judge.
scores.sharpen: Coordinate with the C01 long-lie posts and keep this one strictly about care home equipment, training and the 'do not lift' rules, with the tool quoted exactly.

scores.accuracy_concern: RESTORE2 evaluations are largely uncontrolled; Kane 2017 did not show a significant overall reduction in admissions, and the larger effect in high-engagement homes is an exploratory subgroup.
scores.sharpen: Put the feedback step (the care worker hears what was decided) at the centre of the post and state the INTERACT trial result in plain words.

scores.accuracy_concern: Barker 2017 is cross-sectional and the mortality review and Norwegian study are observational, so no causal verbs; give absolute figures where the papers allow.
scores.sharpen: Open with the request the reader can make ('You can ask to see the same GP each time') and give one plain-number finding from Barker 2017.

scores.accuracy_concern: In Scotland covert medication sits under the Adults with Incapacity Act with a section 47 certificate and the Mental Welfare Commission guide, which may have been updated since 2017; the Kirkevold 2005 prevalence figures are old Norwegian data.
scores.sharpen: State the Scottish legal route explicitly alongside NICE SC1 and keep the crushing warning to one named example (modified-release tablets).

scores.accuracy_concern: The proportion (thought to be about 41 in 100) must be taken from Wolters et al. 2019 with its data year; the classification combines ambulatory care sensitive and other diagnosis groups and involved no case review.
scores.sharpen: Give the verified proportion, then one clearly labelled illustrative case of a resident whose admission fell in a 'potentially avoidable' group and was still right for them.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Moderate agreement' needs a figure from a named validation study (Brundle 2019 or similar); the eFI was developed to predict outcomes in populations; the contract wording on frailty identification must be checked.
scores.sharpen: Give the agreement result in plain words from a named study and keep clear of C05's Clinical Frailty Scale posts.

scores.accuracy_concern: Parkinson's UK's 'within 30 minutes' advice and the NICE NG71 wording on care homes must be verified; the claim that home care visit times often do not match dose times needs a source or should be framed as a check to make.
scores.sharpen: Verify the timing advice and add one concrete home care fix, such as booking the morning visit to the first dose time.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE CG76 and NG67 wording on compliance aids must be quoted exactly; the RPS 2013 statement is older and should be checked for any update.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the 'why are doses being missed?' question so the post reads as a refinement of E169 rather than a contradiction of it.

scores.accuracy_concern: Reported shorter stays come from uncontrolled Sutton data; current use of the Red Bag varies and some areas have stopped, so it must not be presented as a current national standard.
scores.sharpen: Check whether the scheme is still in use before presenting it as a model, and consider folding it into a care home to hospital transfer post in C15.

scores.accuracy_concern: Quote the current edition of the BMA, Resuscitation Council UK and RCN guidance; keep to what CQC 2021 found (concerns about blanket decisions and poor involvement) without implying a prevalence.
scores.sharpen: Coordinate with C19; if it stays here, focus on care home residents specifically and add the question a family can ask when a form appears.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE NG21 is England-only guidance and not a legal entitlement; the short-visit conditions must be quoted exactly.
scores.sharpen: Merge the short-visit rule into C16-02, or give this post a position of its own; as a standalone summary of guidance it lacks an argument.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Irving 2017 UK consultation length is based on older data; NICE NG56 wording on longer appointments must be checked; the 3D trial population included adults of all ages with multimorbidity.
scores.sharpen: Lead with the 3D trial finding (better experience of care, no difference in quality of life), which is a more interesting and defensible hook than generic appointment advice.

scores.accuracy_concern: Home sight test eligibility as described is England-specific (Scotland has free eye examinations for all and its own domiciliary rules); Ornstein 2015 is US data; the UK preventive-care gap for housebound people is unverified and official NHS pages could not be opened.
scores.sharpen: Add the Scottish position on home eye examinations and either find a UK source on housebound patients' routine care or cut that claim.

scores.values_concern: The position on how proactive care should be evaluated is a service judgement; mark it as judgement rather than a finding.
scores.accuracy_concern: Crocker 2024 graded most findings as low or very low certainty and its benefit was on living at home for some combinations only; Stokes 2015 reported secondary care use and some other outcomes, which should be stated accurately.
scores.sharpen: State the certainty of the Crocker 2024 findings in plain words and name one outcome a practice could measure instead of admissions avoided.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check whether the 2016 Cochrane review has been updated; the English rule is that councils must not charge for the first six weeks, and Scotland's arrangements differ; Tuntland 2015 effects were strongest at early follow-up.
scores.sharpen: Phrase the charging rule exactly with the Scottish position noted, and make 'ask for your goals in writing and a review at the end' the closing instruction.

scores.accuracy_concern: Rushcliffe effects must be quoted from Lloyd et al. 2017 and attributed to the package, not to each component; other vanguard sites showed smaller or no differences.
scores.sharpen: Differentiate from C16-06 by focusing on why results varied between vanguard sites, with verified figures from the Improvement Analytics Unit reports.

allocation_reason: Fourteen candidates score 44.5 or more with sound evidence routes and no disqualifying flag, and 27 of 29 clear the strength bar (36 of 50, or about 40 on the formula's true maximum of 55), so the set supports the full 14.
balance_note: Among the top 14, six are for practitioners (C16-01, 10, 11, 15, 17, 27), six for both (04, 16, 20, 21, 23, 28) and only two for the public (07, 26). To lift the public share, swap C16-06 (public, 43.5) and possibly C16-13 (public, 42.5, after evidence checks) in for C16-16 or C16-27. Four of the top 14 are about medicines (11, 17, 20, 21) and should be checked against C06. Only C16-15 is from the Care that works series, so consider C16-14 or C16-29. C16-23 (CPR decisions), C16-14 (long lies), C16-10 (discharge) and C16-08/C16-26 (access and digital exclusion) overlap with C19, C01, C15 and C17 and should be coordinated across categories.
